title: Your net. Their benefit.
narration: A bednet keeps mosquitoes away while you sleep. Insecticide-treated nets can also reduce malaria transmission nearby. So your choice can protect other people. That extra benefit is a positive externality. Remember it this way: private benefit helps you; external benefit helps someone else. Together they make the social benefit.
question: The benefit to neighbors is…
why: An externality is a benefit or cost that spills over to other people.

title: Cheap for you ≠ free to make
narration: A subsidy makes a bednet cheaper for the buyer. It does not erase the cost of making it. Why subsidize? Buyers may consider their own protection but overlook the protection they provide to neighbors. Lowering the price can encourage more use, bringing consumption closer to the socially desirable level.
question: A subsidy directly lowers…
options: the resources needed to produce a net
why: Someone still bears the production cost; the buyer pays less.

title: Random does not mean magic
narration: Random assignment makes treatment and control groups comparable on average before a program. That helps isolate the program’s effect. It does not guarantee identical groups, a positive effect, or statistical significance. Think fair comparison, not guaranteed success. A small effect or a small sample can still produce an imprecise estimate.
question: Random assignment guarantees…
options: none of those; it creates comparability on average
why: Randomization supports a fair comparison, not a particular result.

title: Your $30 trap
narration: You pay ten dollars today and receive forty next year. With a discount factor of one half, that future forty is worth twenty today. Subtract the ten dollar cost. Net present value is ten dollars, not thirty. The order is simple: discount future payments first, then subtract today’s cost.
question: Cost 10 now; receive 60 next year; β = 0.5. NPV?
why: 0.5 × 60 − 10 = 20. Discount first, subtract second.
source: Practice 2nd Partial Exam Questions · Returns to Education lecture

title: Different starts are okay
narration: Difference in differences does not require equal starting levels. It requires parallel trends: without the treatment, both groups would have changed by the same amount. One village can start poorer than another. The key is the path they would have followed without the program, which we cannot directly observe for treated villages.
question: Parallel trends means equal…
why: The assumption concerns untreated changes, not initial levels.

title: Your control group got help
narration: Deworming children can reduce infections beyond their own school. Nearby untreated children may benefit too. Suppose treated outcomes improve by ten and control outcomes improve by three because of spillovers. The difference is seven. That comparison misses the benefit reaching the controls, so it understates the full impact relative to no program.
question: Benefiting the controls can make the comparison…
why: A partially benefited control group is not a no-program benchmark.
source: Health Externalities slides · Posted exam key, cross-school externalities

title: Does paying make you use it?
narration: In Cohen and Dupas, charging more sharply reduced bednet acquisition. Among people who acquired a net, paying more did not clearly increase use. So charging is not a reliable cure for waste. Overall protection depends on both acquisition and use. Even unchanged usage among recipients cannot offset a big fall in how many get nets.
question: The evidence supports…
why: Acquisition falls without a clear offsetting increase in use among recipients.

title: Two gates to protection
narration: Think of protection as two gates. First, get a net. Second, use it. In the worksheet illustration, assume sixty five percent usage. Free distribution gives roughly sixty four protected people per hundred. At forty shillings, it gives about twenty five. These calculations use the worksheet’s usage assumption; they are not separate estimates of the full experiment.
question: Coverage depends on…
why: People must both acquire and use a net to be protected in this calculation.

title: The outcome you cannot see
narration: A causal effect compares what happened with treatment to what would have happened to the same person without it. That second outcome is the counterfactual. We cannot observe both at once. Research designs create a credible comparison to estimate the missing outcome. A before and after change alone may also include unrelated trends.
question: The counterfactual is…
options: the untreated outcome that would have occurred
why: It is the alternative outcome under no treatment.

title: A regression is not a verdict
narration: Before interpreting a regression, read the outcome, units, and comparison group. Then check the coefficient’s sign and uncertainty. Finally ask what design makes the estimate causal. A precise correlation is still not automatically a causal effect. Ability or family resources, for example, can influence both education and earnings.
question: A precise schooling–earnings correlation…
options: still needs a credible causal design
why: Confounding can remain even when estimates are very precise.

title: The DiD subtraction
narration: Treatment wages rise from one forty to one fifty: a gain of ten. Control wages rise from one fifty five to one seventy two: a gain of seventeen. Difference in differences is ten minus seventeen, or negative seven. Treatment wages rose, but less than their estimated counterfactual. A negative effect does not require an observed decline.
question: The treated counterfactual wage is…
why: 140 + the control change of 17 = 157; observed 150 is 7 lower.

title: IV: use an outside nudge
narration: An instrumental variable is an outside nudge that changes the treatment you care about. It must be relevant: it changes treatment. The exclusion restriction says it affects the outcome only through that treatment. An instrument also needs a credible independence argument. A variable that predicts schooling is not enough if it directly changes wages too.
question: A direct instrument-to-wage effect would threaten…
why: Exclusion rules out an outcome effect through another channel.

title: RD: look across the line
narration: Regression discontinuity compares observations just across a cutoff or boundary. The idea is that nearby observations are otherwise comparable, but treatment changes abruptly. The crucial check is whether other outcome determinants remain smooth across the cutoff. Sorting, manipulation, or another policy changing at the same boundary can undermine the design.
question: A threat to RD is…
options: an abrupt change in another important factor
why: Another discontinuity can explain the outcome jump instead of treatment.

title: A loan can reach nonborrowers
narration: Breza and Kinnan study a microfinance credit contraction and its local economic effects. Credit can affect more than borrowers: reduced borrowing can lower demand for local goods and labor. Their evidence includes lower casual wages and earnings. The takeaway is a local economy mechanism, not simply whether an individual borrower’s business earns more.
question: Why can nonborrowers be affected?
options: Spending changes demand for their labor
why: Local demand connects borrowers to other firms and workers.

title: War has different exposures
narration: The war reading distinguishes where fighting occurs, who participates, and who is indirectly exposed. War sites can lose capital, productivity, and output while prices rise. Other countries can be affected through trade and supply chains. Do not treat all war exposure as identical, or describe historical estimates as a randomized experiment.
question: A third country can be affected through…
why: Trade and supply chains transmit economic shocks across borders.

title: History can persist
narration: Nunn connects historical slave exports to poorer later economic performance. The mechanism is persistent damage: insecurity, fragmentation, and weakened institutions can outlast the original slave trade. The empirical challenge is causality, because exposed places may already have differed. Know both the proposed mechanism and the identification strategy, not just the negative correlation.
question: The persistence mechanism emphasizes…
options: a guaranteed effect in every country
why: Historical shocks can alter institutions and social organization for generations.
source: Nunn (2008), assigned Sections I–IV · Consequences of Slavery slides

title: Ruggedness cuts both ways
narration: Rugged terrain can hurt farming, transport, and trade. But in Africa it also helped protect communities from slave raids. Nunn and Puga separate that direct geographic cost from an indirect historical benefit. In an interaction regression, the Africa effect is the baseline ruggedness coefficient plus the Africa interaction, not the interaction alone.
question: The total Africa ruggedness effect is…
why: An interaction modifies the baseline effect; add them for the subgroup total.
source: Nunn–Puga (2012), Ruggedness: The Blessing of Bad Geography in Africa

title: Do not mix up trust
narration: Lowes and Montero compare places across historical Congo concession boundaries. Their findings combine weaker formal institutions with stronger local cooperation and trust among villagers. Those can coexist: people may rely more on community networks when formal institutions fail. Do not turn this into a blanket claim that every historical abuse lowers every kind of trust.
question: The key distinction is…
why: Weak formal governance can coexist with stronger informal support.

title: Profitable, but unaffordable
narration: Schooling is an investment. Its costs include tuition and earnings given up while studying. Benefits may arrive years later. Even when discounted benefits exceed costs, a family may lack cash or access to borrowing today. That is a credit constraint. Profitability and affordability are two different questions.
question: A positive NPV guarantees…
options: neither cash today nor borrowing access
why: A good long-run investment can remain out of reach today.
source: Development Economics, assigned pp. 419–432 · Returns to Education lecture

title: Two years? Discount twice.
narration: Timing matters. If twenty dollars arrives in period two, and the discount factor is one half per period, multiply by one half twice. Twenty becomes five in present value. With a ten dollar cost today, net present value is negative five. The exponent counts periods. The internal rate of return is the rate that makes NPV zero.
question: A payment in period 2 is multiplied by…
why: Discount once for each period until the payment arrives.
source: Practice 2nd Partial Exam Questions · Returns to Education lecture

title: School years ≠ learning
narration: More years in school, more learning, and higher earnings are related but distinct outcomes. Enrollment does not prove skills improved. A wage premium does not automatically identify schooling’s causal return. When reading a result, name the actual outcome: attendance, learning, completed years, or earnings. That keeps your interpretation tied to the evidence.
question: Higher enrollment directly demonstrates…
options: more enrollment, not necessarily more learning
why: Measure each outcome rather than treating them as interchangeable.
source: Development Economics pp. 419–432 · Returns to Education slides

title: Why subsidize schooling?
narration: Education can benefit coworkers and other people beyond the student. If a student counts only personal gains, they may invest less than society would prefer. A subsidy can help align the private decision with the social benefit. In the course’s numerical example, transfers can make education worthwhile while leaving other affected parties better off.
question: Positive education externalities imply private benefits can be…
why: Social benefit includes the student’s benefit plus external benefits.
source: Practice 2nd Partial Exam Questions, parts c–h

title: What Progresa identifies
narration: Progresa gave poor families cash transfers conditional on schooling. A randomized village rollout supports estimating the program’s effect. But comparing the program with no program does not isolate conditionality itself. To learn the extra effect of the condition, you would need a suitable comparison with unconditional transfers. Separate the package’s effect from each component’s effect.
question: Program versus no program identifies…
why: Cash and conditions change together, so their separate effects are not isolated.

title: Duflo: place × age
narration: Duflo studies Indonesia’s large school construction program. Compare regions receiving different construction intensity, and cohorts young enough to benefit versus older cohorts. Combining place and age exposure helps estimate the schooling effect. The design needs a credible counterfactual for how cohort differences would evolve without the program. Building schools was not randomly assigned.
question: The design combines…
why: The comparison uses both where and when people were exposed.

title: IV is a ratio
narration: Here is the Duflo IV calculation from the review. Divide the reduced form wage effect, point zero one four seven, by the first stage schooling effect, point one nine six. You get point zero seven five: about seven and a half percent per additional school year. Use compatible estimates from the same specification and sample.
question: The IV ratio is…
options: first stage divided by reduced form
reduced form divided by first stage
why: Divide the outcome effect of the instrument by its treatment effect.

title: Health gains ≠ test-score gains
narration: Miguel and Kremer study school-based deworming with a phased rollout. Attendance improves, with absenteeism reduced by roughly one quarter, but test-score gains are not clearly established in the study. A quarter reduction in absence is not twenty five percentage points. Always distinguish relative changes, percentage points, and the outcome actually measured.
question: A 25% reduction from 20% absenteeism gives…
why: One quarter of 20 is 5; 20 minus 5 equals 15 percent.
source: Miguel–Kremer (2004), assigned Sections 1–3 · Health Externalities lecture

title: Pay for the vaccine market
narration: An advance market commitment promises a market for qualifying vaccines. Firms may hesitate to invest when demand or future payment is uncertain. A credible commitment can encourage supply investment. This is a pull incentive: reward delivery of the desired product. It differs from simply paying research costs upfront, which is a push incentive.
question: An AMC is mainly a…
why: The promised future market rewards supplying a qualifying vaccine.

title: Cheapest is not always best
narration: For an advance market commitment, a very low supplier reward can discourage participation or investment. A very high reward uses resources that could buy health elsewhere. Recipient copayments can also reduce uptake if set too high. The goal is a useful balance of supply incentives, adoption, and health gains per resource spent.
question: Why not always minimize the supplier payment?
why: Suppliers need enough expected return to invest and participate.

title: Compare what you give up
narration: Country A gives up two units of food to make a shirt. Country B gives up five. A has comparative advantage in shirts because its opportunity cost is lower. Absolute advantage asks who uses fewer resources. Comparative advantage asks who sacrifices less of the other good. Trade patterns depend on that relative sacrifice.
question: A has comparative advantage because…
options: it sells at a higher price
why: Two food forgone is a lower opportunity cost than five.

title: The price tells you what to make
narration: In the Ricardian model, compare a good’s relative price with its opportunity cost. If the market pays more for a shirt than the food you give up making it, shirt production is attractive. With constant opportunity costs, specialization can occur. If the relative price equals opportunity cost, producing both goods can be consistent with equilibrium.
question: At a relative price above its opportunity cost, a good becomes…
why: The value gained exceeds the value of what production sacrifices.
source: Ricardo chapter, production possibilities and gains from trade

title: Produce here. Consume there.
narration: In the practice example, ten units of labor can make ten manufactured goods. At a world price of two food per manufactured good, export five manufactured goods for ten food. Consumption is five manufactured goods plus ten food. Trade separates what the country produces from what it consumes, expanding its consumption possibilities.
question: Exporting 5 M at 2 food per M buys…
why: Five times two equals ten units of food.
source: Posted second partial exam answer key, Ricardo problem d–g

title: Wages must fit productivity
beats: Low wages alone do not decide
narration: Low wages do not automatically mean low production costs. In the Ricardian model, unit labor cost is the wage times labor needed per unit. A high wage country can remain competitive when workers are sufficiently productive. Transport costs also keep some goods nontraded. Compare wage and productivity together, not wages alone.
question: Unit labor cost equals…
why: Productivity determines how much labor is needed for each unit.
source: Ricardo chapter, world equilibrium, relative wages and many goods

title: A country gains. Who loses?
narration: In the specific factors model, labor moves between sectors, while some factors are stuck. When the relative price of an export good rises, the factor specific to that sector gains. The other sector’s specific factor loses. Labor’s real income effect depends on consumption prices. Aggregate gains from trade do not mean every person gains.
question: Aggregate gains from trade imply…
options: the country can gain while some people lose
why: Total gains and distributional effects are different questions.
source: Trade: Specific Factors Model, redistributive effects

title: Tariff money is not all a loss
narration: An import tariff raises the domestic price in a small country while imports continue. Consumers lose, domestic producers gain, and government collects revenue. Transfers are not all deadweight loss. The efficiency losses come from extra costly domestic production and reduced valuable consumption. If the tariff eliminates imports completely, tariff revenue is zero.
question: A tariff that stops all imports collects…
why: Revenue equals tax per unit times remaining imports; zero imports means zero revenue.
source: Posted second partial exam answer key, tariff question

title: An export tax pushes price down
narration: For a small exporting country, a fifteen percent export tax lowers the domestic price to eighty five percent of the world price while exports continue. Producers receive less and supply less. Domestic consumers buy more. Exports shrink. Government revenue is the tax per unit times remaining exports, not the quantity exported before the tax.
question: An export tax generally makes domestic consumers face…
why: Exporters’ after-tax return determines the lower domestic price in this setup.
source: Practice 2nd Partial Exam Questions, Argentina beef export tax

title: Free stove. Paid back in fuel.
narration: A cookstove can save fuel yet remain unaffordable upfront. A firm might supply it free and recover its cost through later fuel sales. In the example, the household saves ten cents a day and the firm captures forty cents of daily margin. But cheaper competing fuel can undermine repayment. Check discounted margins, not just total sales.
question: What threatens the financing model?
options: Competitors undercutting the future fuel price
why: If customers switch suppliers, the firm may not recover its upfront stove cost.
source: Practice 2nd Partial Exam Questions, Inyenyeri financing model
